title: Project Overview
description: Start with the README to learn what this project is: a classic Dots & Boxes game built with React Native + Expo + TypeScript, offering local 2-player play, a 3-tier AI opponent, real-time online multiplayer over Firebase Firestore, a coin reward system, and an unlockable theme shop. Its 20 sections cover features, tech stack, project structure, Firebase setup, and the AI difficulty tiers, giving you the roadmap for the rest of this tour. Pay attention to the key design constraint it calls out: useOnlineGame returns the same shape as useGameEngine so the rendering components work unchanged for both modes.

title: App Entry & Theme Bootstrap
description: The Expo Router root layout is the very first thing that runs: it loads the custom handwritten fonts, restores the persisted theme from AsyncStorage, and wraps the entire app in a ThemeContext before rendering the navigation Stack. Because Expo Router uses file-based routing, _layout.tsx implicitly hands control to app/index.tsx (the home screen) once setup completes. This is where the project's global concerns — fonts and theming — are established before any screen renders.
languageLesson: Expo Router uses file-based routing: files in the app/ directory become routes, and a special _layout.tsx file wraps all sibling routes — the React Native equivalent of a layout component that persists across navigation.

title: Home & Settings Screen
description: app/index.tsx is the home screen and the BFS root of the codebase — it has the broadest reach, pulling in the most modules. From here players choose game mode (2-player, vs AI, online), grid size, names, timer, and difficulty; it also shows stats and the coin balance, and drives the Quick Match matchmaking flow before routing into the appropriate game screen. Building on the theme context from Step 2, this screen is the hub that branches into every feature the README described.

title: Shared Types Foundation
description: game.types.ts is the single most depended-upon file in the project (highest fan-in by far), making it the vocabulary the entire app speaks. It declares GameState, GameMode (including 'online'), Line, Player, board owner arrays, and the config and event interfaces consumed by hooks, components, services, and screens alike. Understanding these types now makes every later step easier, because they are the contract that lets local and online play share the same components.
languageLesson: TypeScript discriminated unions (e.g. a GameMode tagging GameState) let the compiler narrow behavior per mode, while the firebase-shim.d.ts ambient declaration file re-declares firebase/* modules so TS can resolve the v10 web SDK under node moduleResolution.

title: Pure Game Logic & AI
description: The domain layer is pure and side-effect free, which makes it the most testable and reusable part of the codebase. gameHelpers.ts builds the initial board, detects completed boxes, enumerates available lines, simulates a move, and snapshots state for undo — the rules of Dots & Boxes expressed as plain functions. aiPlayer.ts builds directly on those helpers, exposing a single getAIMove with three tiers: easy (random), medium (heuristic), and hard (minimax with alpha-beta pruning and chain avoidance).
languageLesson: Keeping game rules and AI as pure functions (no React, no Firebase) means the same logic powers local play, AI play, and could be tested in isolation — a clean separation of domain logic from I/O.

title: The Shared Game-Engine Contract
description: This is the architectural keystone the README highlighted. useGameEngine.ts drives local 2-player and vs-AI games — board state, turn switching, scoring, undo, per-turn timer, and AI move scheduling — consuming the pure logic from Step 5. useOnlineGame.ts does the same job over Firestore (subscribing to a room document and reconstructing board state) yet deliberately returns the exact same shape. Because the two hooks are interface-compatible, the rendering components in Step 7 work unchanged for both modes.
languageLesson: Two hooks exposing an identical return shape is a form of duck-typed polymorphism: the consuming components depend on the shape, not the implementation, so swapping local for online play requires zero component changes.

title: Rendering: Board & Score Bar
description: These presentational components consume the hook contract from Step 6 and never care whether the data is local or online. GameBoard.tsx is an SVG-based board that draws dots, lines, and filled boxes, highlights the last move and newly captured boxes, and emits onLineTap for input. ScoreBar.tsx is the header showing both players' names and scores, the active-turn indicator, the AI-thinking state, and a countdown timer when enabled. Together they are the visual surface every game mode shares.

title: Local & Online Game Screens
description: Now the pieces come together at the screen level. game.tsx wires useGameEngine to GameBoard and ScoreBar for local and AI play, plays sound effects, and awards coins and records stats on game end. online-game.tsx does the parallel job with useOnlineGame, disabling input when it is not the player's turn and awarding coins on result. Seeing both screens side by side makes the shared-contract payoff concrete: nearly identical screens, different data sources.

title: Firebase Service Foundation
description: firebase.ts is the third-highest fan-in file and the gateway to all backend features: it initializes the Firebase web SDK app, Firestore, and anonymous auth, exporting shared instances plus getAnonymousUid(). gameRoom.ts builds on it to manage the online room lifecycle — code generation, board flatten/unflatten serialization, create/join, move application, turn skipping, abandon, and rematch — which is exactly what useOnlineGame from Step 6 subscribes to. This layer is where the real-time multiplayer the README promised actually lives.

title: Lobby & Matchmaking
description: lobby.tsx is the entry into online play: it lets players create or join a room by 6-character code, validates input, and navigates into online-game.tsx once a match exists. matchmaking.ts powers the Quick Match flow surfaced on the home screen (Step 3), managing a Firestore queue — joining, cancelling, listening for a match, scanning the waiting pool, and atomically pairing two players into a room via a transaction. Building on the room service from Step 9, this step closes the loop on how two strangers end up in the same game.

title: Coins, Shop & Leaderboard
description: This is the economy layer the README's reward table described. coins.ts (second-highest fan-in among services) handles user profile bootstrap, balance read/subscribe, awarding and spending coins, the daily bonus, online-result rewards, and theme ownership/activation. shop.tsx spends coins to purchase and activate themes, while leaderboard.ts queries Firestore for the top users by coin balance and leaderboard.tsx renders that ranking, highlighting the current user. Together they turn winning games into progression.

title: Theme System & Local Storage
description: These two foundations underpin personalization and persistence. useTheme.ts (second-highest fan-in overall) defines the ThemeTokens interface, the THEMES token map (parchment, neon, chalkboard, blueprint), display metadata, and the ThemeContext that Step 2 populated — every component reads the active theme through its useTheme hook. storage.ts is the AsyncStorage-backed layer that persists local preferences, win/loss stats, the tutorial-seen flag, and the sound preference, complementing the Firestore-backed coin and theme state.

title: Firestore Security Rules
description: firestore.rules is the trust boundary protecting everything in the service layer (Steps 9-11). It governs access to the rooms, matchmaking, users, and coinTransactions collections: authenticated reads/writes for rooms and matchmaking, owner-scoped user documents, and read-only audit-trail coin transactions so balances can't be forged client-side. This is how the backend stays safe even though all game logic runs on untrusted clients.
languageLesson: Firestore security rules run server-side on every read/write: making coinTransactions read-only from clients turns the ledger into a tamper-proof audit trail, since balances are derived from server-controlled writes rather than client claims.

title: Standalone Web PWA
description: Separate from the Expo app, index.html is a self-contained single-file implementation of Dots & Boxes with all HTML, CSS, and JavaScript inlined — no build step, no dependencies, runs directly in a browser. sw.js is its service worker (precache on install, cache cleanup on activate, cache-first for local assets, network-first for Google Fonts) and manifest.json declares the PWA metadata so it can install to a home screen. This is the lightweight, dependency-free counterpart to the full mobile app.
languageLesson: A service worker is a background script that intercepts network requests, enabling offline play via caching strategies — cache-first for your own assets (instant, offline-safe) versus network-first for third-party resources (always fresh when online).

title: Build & Deployment Config
description: The capstone covers how the project is configured and shipped. package.json declares the start/android/ios/web scripts and runtime dependencies (Expo, Expo Router, Firebase, AsyncStorage); tsconfig.json sets the @/* path alias and the node moduleResolution that Firebase v10 needs; app.json and eas.json configure the Expo app and EAS production builds; while netlify.toml handles hosting the standalone web PWA from Step 14. These files tie together everything you have seen into runnable, deployable artifacts.
